q: Who is the author of the story "Madam Rides the Bus"?
o: Gavin Maxwell
Vallikkannan
Lucio Rodrigues
Anton Chekhov
e: Vallikkannan is the author of "Madam Rides the Bus" (translated from Tamil by K.S. Sundaram).

q: What was Valli’s full name and how old was she?
o: Vineeta, six years old
Vandana, twelve years old
Valliammai, eight years old
Vasundhara, ten years old
e: The story introduces Valliammai, called Valli for short, as an eight-year-old girl.

q: What was Valli’s favourite pastime? [JAC 2019]
o: Standing in the front doorway of her house watching what happened in the street outside
Swimming in a river
Painting portraits
Playing cards indoors
e: Having no playmates of her own age on her street, her favourite pastime was standing in the front doorway watching the street outside.

q: How far was the nearest town from Valli’s village?
o: Two miles
Six miles
Twenty miles
Fifty miles
e: Through careful listening, Valli learned that the town was six miles from her village.

q: What was the one-way bus fare from Valli’s village to the town?
o: One rupee
Ten paise
Thirty paise
Sixty paise
e: The one-way fare was thirty paise, so Valli saved sixty paise for the round trip.

q: How long did the bus trip to the town take one way?
o: Two hours
Three hours
Fifteen minutes
Forty-five minutes
e: The trip to the town took forty-five minutes one way.

q: How much money did Valli finally manage to save for her round-trip bus journey?
o: Sixty paise
Ninety paise
Two rupees
Thirty paise
e: By resisting peppermints, toys, balloons, and even the merry-go-round, Valli saved sixty paise.

q: What nickname did the jolly bus conductor give Valli?
o: Princess
Madam
Mini
Queen
e: When Valli proudly insisted she could get on by herself, the jolly conductor playfully addressed her as "Madam".

q: Why did Valli choose the afternoon hours between one and four o’clock for her bus ride?
o: Because roads closed at night
Because buses did not run in the morning
Because her mother regularly took an afternoon nap after lunch during those hours
Because tickets cost more in the evening
e: Her mother always napped from about one to four after lunch, giving Valli an opportunity to slip out unnoticed.

q: How was the outside of the new bus painted?
o: Blue and black
Plain brown
Dark red and yellow
Gleaming white with some green stripes along the sides
e: It was a new bus, its outside painted a gleaming white with some green stripes along the sides.

q: Which sight on the way to town made Valli laugh until there were tears in her eyes?
o: A young cow, tail high in the air, galloping right in front of the bus
A monkey climbing a pole
The driver singing loudly
The conductor tripping
e: A young cow, frightened by the loud honking, kept galloping right in front of the bus with its tail high in the air, making Valli laugh till tears filled her eyes.

q: Why was Valli suddenly overcome with sadness on the return journey?
o: She lost her return fare
She saw the same lovable young cow lying dead in a pool of blood, struck by a fast vehicle
The conductor scolded her
Heavy rain ruined her view
e: Seeing the same young cow she had laughed at earlier lying dead and bloodied by the roadside deeply dampened Valli’s spirits.

q: At what time did the bus reach back to Valli’s village on the return trip?
o: Six ten
Two o’clock
Three forty
Five o’clock
e: The bus reached her village at three forty, and Valli ran straight home.

q: At the village fair, which strong temptation did Valli suppress in order to save money for the bus ride?
o: Circus tent
Puppet show
Elephant ride
Riding the merry-go-round
e: Even with money in hand at the village fair, she resolutely stifled her desire to ride the merry-go-round.

q: When the bus reached town and the conductor offered to buy Valli a cold drink as a treat, how did she respond?
o: She politely but firmly refused the treat
She ran off into the market
She borrowed money from him
She accepted two drinks eagerly
e: Self-respecting Valli firmly declined his offer ("No, thank you"), refusing any free favours.

q: Who wrote the poem "The Tale of Custard the Dragon"?
o: Walt Whitman
Ogden Nash
Carl Sandburg
Robert Frost
e: American poet Ogden Nash wrote the humorous ballad "The Tale of Custard the Dragon".

q: Where did Belinda live with her pets in "The Tale of Custard the Dragon"? [JAC 2019]
o: On a sailing boat
In a large black castle
In a little white house
In a high treehouse
e: The opening line states: "Belinda lived in a little white house..."

q: Who was Custard, and what did he always cry for? [JAC 2019, 2023]
o: A black kitten; warm milk
A grey mouse; cheese
A yellow dog; a bone
A little pet dragon; a nice safe cage
e: Custard was Belinda’s little pet dragon, mocked as a coward because he constantly cried for a nice safe cage.

q: Match Belinda’s pets correctly in "The Tale of Custard the Dragon":
o: Ink: black kitten; Blink: grey mouse; Mustard: yellow dog; Custard: pet dragon
Mustard: mouse; Custard: kitten; Ink: lion
Blink: dragon; Ink: bear; Mustard: fish
Ink: yellow dog; Blink: black kitten
e: Belinda had a little black kitten (Ink), little grey mouse (Blink), little yellow dog (Mustard), and pet dragon (Custard).

q: What ironic nickname did Ink, Blink, and Mustard rudely call Custard?
o: Robin Hood
Percival
Lancelot
Alexander
e: Ink, Blink, and Mustard rudely called him "Percival" (mockingly after King Arthur’s brave knight Sir Percival).

q: When the pirate climbed through the window, what did he hold between his teeth?
o: A coiled rope
A gold coin
A bright cutlass
A burning torch
e: Holding pistols in both hands, the black-bearded pirate with a wooden leg held a bright cutlass between his teeth.

q: What did Custard ultimately do to the invading pirate?
o: Tossed him out of the roof
Made friends with him
Handed him over to the police
Gobbled him up, every single bit
e: After the pirate’s two shots missed, Custard attacked fiercely and "gobbled him, every bit."

q: What were on Custard’s toes according to the poem?
o: Realio, trulio daggers on his toes
Glass bangles
Silver bells
Soft velvet pads
e: Besides fireplace mouth and chimney nose, Custard had "realio, trulio daggers on his toes."

q: What colour was Belinda’s little wagon in "The Tale of Custard the Dragon"?
o: Blue
Red
Green
Black
e: The opening stanza lists "a little yellow dog and a little red wagon."

q: How did Mustard the yellow dog react when the pirate broke in?
o: He danced on the table
He bit the pirate’s wooden leg
He fled with a terrified yelp
He fired back with pistols
e: Though earlier compared to a tiger in a rage, Mustard immediately fled with a terrified yelp.

q: How did Ink and Blink react when the pirate appeared?
o: They leaped off the balcony
They laughed at the pirate
They charged forward bravely
Ink trickled down to the bottom of the household and Blink strategically mouseholed
e: Ink trickled down to the bottom of the house while Blink "strategically mouseholed" into shelter.

q: What was the elderly woman sitting next to Valli on the bus chewing?
o: Betel nut
Chocolate
Basil leaves
Cardamom pods
e: The woman had big ear-lobe holes, ugly earrings, and was chewing betel nut whose juice threatened to spill over her lips.

q: Whom was Valli’s mother talking with when Valli returned from her bus ride?
o: The village postman
An aunt from South Street, who was a real chatterbox
The school headmistress
The bus driver
e: Her mother was chatting with one of Valli’s aunts from South Street, described as "a real chatterbox."

q: What did the pirate gulp from his pocket flagon before firing at Custard?
o: Lemonade
Cold water
Some grog
Hot tea
e: Gaping in shock at Custard’s charge, the pirate "gulped some grog from his pocket flagon" and fired two bullets.

q: After Custard ate the pirate, how brave did Mustard claim he would have been had he not been "flustered"?
o: Half as brave
Not brave at all
Twice as brave
Four times as brave
e: Mustard boasted he would have been twice as brave if he hadn’t been flustered, while Ink and Blink claimed to be three times as brave.

q: What was the most fascinating sight of all for Valli while watching from her front doorway?
o: The bus that travelled between her village and the nearest town, filled each hour with new passengers
Cricket matches nearby
The village sweetshop
Aeroplanes flying overhead
e: The bus passing every hour with a fresh set of passengers was a source of unending joy for Valli.

q: Who casually remarked in Valli’s hearing that thirty paise was "almost nothing at all"?
o: Her mother
A well-dressed man
The bus driver
The village watchman
e: A well-dressed man called thirty paise "almost nothing at all," though to Valli it seemed a small fortune.

q: What exact time-table had Valli calculated before boarding the bus?
o: Catching the 5 p.m. express
Taking the 9 a.m. bus and returning at 8 p.m.
Taking the one-o’clock bus, reaching town at 1:45, staying seated, and returning around 2:45
Walking at dawn
e: She figured out that taking the 1:00 p.m. bus would reach town at 1:45 and bring her home around 2:45 while her mother still napped.

q: What did Valli say when the conductor stretched out a hand to help her board the bus?
o: "Give me a free ticket."
"Put me near the driver."
"Thank you, please lift me up."
"I can get on by myself. You don’t have to help me."
e: Independent Valli retorted: "I can get on by myself. You don’t have to help me."

q: How did Valli reply to the elderly man who called her "child" and told her to sit down?
o: "There’s nobody here who’s a child. I’ve paid my thirty paise like everyone else."
"I am the driver’s daughter."
"I cannot reach the cushion."
She quietly sat down in embarrassment
e: Irritated at being called "child", Valli snapped that nobody there was a child since she had paid her full thirty paise like everyone else.

q: Why did Valli have to stand up on her seat during the bus ride?
o: The seat cushion was torn
A canvas blind covered the lower part of her window, blocking her view when seated
The conductor forbade her from sitting
Another passenger pushed her off
e: A canvas blind covered the lower half of her window, so she stood up on her seat to see past it.

q: What scenic sights beyond the canal did Valli see from the bus window?
o: Coal mines and chimneys
Snow peaks and camels
Palm trees, grassland, distant mountains, and the blue, blue sky
Ocean waves and ships
e: Beyond the canal lay palm trees, grassland, distant mountains, and the blue sky, while acres of green fields stretched on the other side.

q: What stood directly in front of Valli above the windshield inside the new bus?
o: A radio box
A garland of marigolds
A brass fan
A beautiful clock
e: Overhead bars shone like silver, and directly in front of her, above the windshield, was a beautiful clock.

q: What did the bus pass before entering the busy street of the town?
o: A railway level-crossing
A dense pine forest
An airfield
A suspension bridge
e: The bus passed a railway level-crossing where a train rushed past before entering a wide thoroughfare in town.

q: Why did Valli refuse to get off the bus to look around the bright shops in town?
o: She felt afraid to go alone in the crowd and had only thirty paise left for the return ticket
Shops were closed for a holiday
She had twisted her ankle
The conductor locked the bus doors
e: She was too afraid to wander around alone, had just enough money for her return ticket, and had come strictly for the bus ride.

q: When Valli returned home and heard her mother and aunt talking about the outside world, how did she react?
o: She scolded her aunt
She confessed her adventure tearfully
She merely smiled mysteriously and casually agreed without letting them understand why
She ran straight under the bed
e: Valli just smiled to herself and casually agreed, keeping her thrilling afternoon adventure a complete secret.

q: What amusing reply did Valli give when the conductor teased her and everyone laughed as she stood up?
o: She threw her ticket out
She jumped off mid-route
She burst into tears
She firmly held her ground, insisting she was no child and had paid her full thirty paise
e: Instead of shrinking back when passengers laughed, Valli stood proudly on her rights as a full-fare-paying passenger.

q: How did Belinda, Ink, Blink, and Mustard boast of their courage before the pirate attacked?
o: Belinda like a lamb and Mustard like a rabbit
Ink like an elephant and Blink like a whale
They all admitted being terrified
Belinda as brave as a barrel full of bears, Ink and Blink chasing lions down stairs, and Mustard like a tiger in a rage
e: Stanza 4 exaggerates their boasts: Belinda like a barrel of bears, Ink and Blink chasing lions, and Mustard like a furious tiger.

q: With which objects are Custard’s mouth and nose compared in the poem?
o: A ball and a bat
A mouth like a fireplace and a chimney for a nose
A rosebud and a leaf
A silver bell and whistle
e: Fire-breathing Custard is described as having a "mouth like a fireplace" and a "chimney for a nose."

q: How did Belinda and the other pets tease Custard inside the little red wagon?
o: They tied him to the gate
They splashed him with icy water
Belinda tickled him unmercifully while Ink, Blink, and Mustard rudely called him Percival and laughed
They starved him for days
e: Belinda tickled him unmercifully while the other three sat in the little red wagon laughing and calling him Percival.

q: What happened right before they saw the pirate climbing in the "winda"?
o: Lightning struck the roof
Custard sang a lullaby
The doorbell rang thrice
They heard a nasty sound; Mustard growled, Ink cried "Meowch!", and Belinda cried "Ooh!"
e: With comical sounds ("Meowch!" and "Ooh!"), all looked around to see a pirate climbing in the window.

q: Which two similes describe Custard’s fierce attack on the pirate?
o: Clashed his tail like irons in a dungeon and went at the pirate like a robin at a worm
Roared like thunder and flowed like water
Squeaked like a frightened mouse
Swayed like a leaf and crawled like a turtle
e: He snorted like an engine, clashed his tail like irons in a dungeon, and charged like a robin at a worm.

q: How did Belinda, Mustard, Ink, and Blink celebrate immediately after Custard gobbled up the pirate?
o: They packed up and left the house
Belinda embraced him, Mustard licked him, and Ink and Blink gyrated in glee around him
They locked him inside a cage
They called the coast guard
e: Belinda embraced him, Mustard licked him, nobody mourned the pirate, and Ink and Blink gyrated around the dragon in glee.

q: When Ink, Blink, and Mustard claimed afterward they were twice or thrice as brave, what did Custard reply?
o: "Give me a crown of gold."
"You are all shameless cowards!"
"I quite agree that everybody is braver than me."
"I am now king of this house!"
e: True to his gentle, unboastful nature, Custard calmly agreed that everyone else was braver than him.

q: Why do the closing stanzas of "The Tale of Custard the Dragon" repeat the opening stanzas in the present tense?
o: To transform the ballad into a tragedy
Because the pirate escaped alive
Because the poet ran out of rhymes
To show life returned to its comic status quo—the boasts continue unchanged while humble Custard still longs for safety
e: Shifting from past to present tense underscores how little people’s boasting changes despite proof of who the true hero is.

q: What qualities did Valli exercise over "many days and months" before actually taking the bus ride?
o: Careful listening, discreet questioning, and patient financial/schedule planning
Stealing coins from neighbours
Quarrelling with her mother
Reckless haste
e: Far from acting impulsively, Valli spent months listening carefully, asking discreet questions, and calculating every paisa and minute.

q: Why wasn’t Valli worried when the conductor warned her that her mother might get worried?
o: She knew her mother’s 1–4 p.m. nap routine ensured she wouldn’t be missed yet
She had left a detailed note
She never planned to return
Her mother was out of town
e: She had carefully timed her trip within her mother’s regular afternoon nap from one to four o’clock.

q: How did most of the passengers on the bus treat eight-year-old Valli?
o: Passengers demanded her seat
They tried to push her off
The conductor was jovial and kind, while elders showed protective concern for her safety
Everyone ignored her completely
e: Despite annoying independent Valli, the elders showed parental concern while the jolly conductor looked out for her playfully.

q: What harsh truth of life did Valli confront through the contrast between the galloping cow and its dead body?
o: That village roads are wider than town streets
That cows never cross highways
That buses travel too slowly
How fragile and sudden the boundary is between vibrant life and unexpected death
e: Seeing the joyful creature reduced to a lifeless corpse within an hour gave young Valli her first sobering glimpse of mortality.

q: Why does Ogden Nash use invented or altered spellings like "realio, trulio" and "winda" in "The Tale of Custard the Dragon"?
o: As comic poetic licence to create humour, playful rhythm, and rhyme (e.g., "winda" rhyming with "Belinda")
Due to printing press errors
To confuse grammar teachers
Because he didn’t know standard spelling
e: Ogden Nash uses poetic licence—altering "window" to "winda" to rhyme humorously with "Belinda", adding light comic charm.

q: What irony lies in Ink, Blink, and Mustard calling Custard a coward despite his physical features?
o: Custard looked like a harmless caterpillar
Custard possessed fearsome teeth, spikes, scales, and dagger-claws, yet the tiny boastful pets called him cowardly
Custard could never breathe fire
Ink and Blink were larger than dragons
e: Equipped with formidable natural weaponry, gentle Custard wanted peace while tiny powerless pets mocked him with empty boasts.

q: What secret did Valli carefully keep from her mother upon reaching home at 3:40 p.m.?
o: That she disliked her aunt
That she had lost her schoolbag
Her secret solo afternoon bus expedition to the town and back
That she bought expensive sweets
e: Knowing her mother would never allow an eight-year-old to travel alone, she kept her entire excursion secret.

q: Why is Valli’s mother’s remark—"So many things in our midst and in the world outside... how can we possibly know about everything?"—ironic to the reader?
o: Because the aunt came from London
Because no buses ever passed that street
Because the mother unknowingly stated a truth right after Valli had secretly taken a solo bus ride while she napped
Because the mother had never stepped outdoors
e: It creates delightful dramatic irony: the mother speaks generally without realising Valli just returned from a secret adventure under her roof.

q: What figure of speech is used in "Ink and Blink chased lions down the stairs"?
o: Understatement
Oxymoron
Euphemism
Hyperbole (exaggeration)
e: Claiming a tiny kitten and grey mouse chased lions down the stairs is clear humorous Hyperbole.

q: How did the round-trip bus journey mature young Valli emotionally?
o: She started fighting with street children
Alongside pride in independence, she gained sobering awareness of life’s beauty paired with sudden death and mystery
She vowed never to leave her house again
She began hating all animals
e: Starting in playful excitement, the journey leaves Valli wiser—balancing pride in self-reliance with sobering awe at life and death.

q: In "she stifled a strong desire to ride the merry-go-round", what does "stifled" mean?
o: Completely forgot
Shouted aloud enthusiastically
Suppressed or held back firmly
Shared with friends
e: "Stifled" means suppressed or kept under firm control—Valli curbed her impulse to protect her bus savings.

q: Why did Valli find the elderly woman passenger sitting beside her "repulsive"?
o: Because she took Valli’s window seat
Because she offered peppermints
Because she spoke another dialect
Because of her big ear-lobe holes, ugly earrings, and betel-nut juice threatening to spill over her lips
e: Fastidious Valli felt repelled by the ugly earrings and dribbling betel-nut juice, keeping her replies curt.

q: What trait of Valli stands out most sharply when she tells the conductor, "Never mind, I can get on by myself"?
o: Fierce self-respect and determination to be independent
Extreme shyness
Fear of strangers
Quiet obedience
e: Refusing assistance shows her fierce pride, self-confidence, and eagerness to be treated as a capable grown-up.

q: Why does Vallikkannan describe the bus’s gleaming white paint, silver bars, clock, and soft seats in such vivid sensory detail?
o: To let the reader experience the magic and wonder of a brand-new bus through an eight-year-old’s fascinated eyes
To advertise a bus manufacturer
To prove the conductor owned the bus
To distract from the village scenery
e: Viewing the polished bus through young Valli’s wide-eyed amazement captures the sheer thrill of her long-awaited dream.

q: What does the conductor’s playful banter ("May we start now, madam?" / "Don’t be angry with me, fine madam") reveal about his character?
o: He disliked lonely passengers
He mocked children cruelly
He was warm-hearted, humorous, and tactful—honouring Valli’s grown-up pride with gentle teasing
He intended to cheat her out of change
e: Recognising Valli’s fierce pride, he kindly humoured her grown-up persona while quietly looking out for her safety.

q: When Valli explains she rode the bus just on a "whim", what does "whim" mean?
o: A bitter punishment
A business contract
A strict legal duty
A sudden, playful urge or fancy
e: "Whim" means a sudden wish or fancy—Valli casually downplayed months of planning with a cool remark.

q: How did encountering the dead cow on the return journey abruptly alter Valli’s mood?
o: Her enthusiasm evaporated in grief, and she sat glued to her seat unwilling to look outside
She leaped off the moving bus
She demanded a refund
She clapped and laughed again
e: Overcome by the stark horror of death, Valli lost all desire to gaze out the window for the rest of the trip.

q: Identify the pair of poetic devices used in "Mouth like a fireplace, chimney for a nose" from "The Tale of Custard the Dragon":
o: Metaphor followed by Simile
Simile ("like a fireplace") followed by Metaphor ("chimney for a nose")
Two examples of Personification
Two examples of Pun
e: "Mouth like a fireplace" uses "like" (Simile), whereas "chimney for a nose" directly equates the nose to a chimney (Metaphor).

q: Which poetic device and contrast are highlighted in "he went at the pirate like a robin at a worm"?
o: Pure alliteration with no visual meaning
Simile—it humorously reduces the menacing pirate to a helpless worm easily snapped up by Custard
Personification turning the pirate into a tree
Oxymoron showing Custard retreated
e: The Simile humorously contrasts the heavily armed pirate’s downfall—snapped up as effortlessly as a worm by a robin.

q: Which combination of poetic devices appears in "clashed his tail like irons in a dungeon"?
o: Rhetorical question
Euphemism
Onomatopoeia/auditory imagery ("clashed") and Simile ("like irons")
Pure irony
e: "Clashed" (along with clatter/clank) creates vivid sound imagery/onomatopoeia, while "like irons in a dungeon" forms a powerful Simile.

q: What poetic genre does "The Tale of Custard the Dragon" belong to, and what is its stanza rhyme scheme?
o: Humorous Ballad, AABB
Sonnet, ABBA
Free verse, unrhymed
Elegy, ABAB
e: It is a humorous ballad (narrative poem) written in four-line stanzas following a steady AABB rhyme scheme.

q: What literary device is at work when Ink, Blink, and Mustard rudely call Custard "Percival"?
o: Allusion and Irony—mocking a timid-seeming dragon with the name of King Arthur’s legendary knight Sir Percival
Onomatopoeia
Hyperbole
Pastoral setting
e: Calling an apparent coward by the name of brave knight Sir Percival is an ironic literary allusion—doubly ironic when Custard turns out to be the real hero.

q: What does the household’s reaction to the pirate ("paled", "fled", "trickled", "mouseholed") expose about their earlier boasts?
o: That it was too dark to notice him
That loud boasts and show-off bravery vanish the instant real danger strikes
That the pirate was merely a toy
That they politely stepped aside for Custard
e: Those who boasted of lion-chasing courage collapsed in panic when genuine danger stepped through the window.

q: In "Ink and Blink in glee did gyrate / Around the dragon that ate the pirate", what does "gyrate" mean?
o: Flee weeping
Fall fast asleep
Sit motionless in fear
Move or spin rapidly in circles (dance around in joy)
e: "Gyrate" means to whirl or move in circles—Ink and Blink danced happily around the victorious dragon.

q: What moral lesson does Valli’s refusal of the conductor’s free cold-drink offer demonstrate?
o: Self-restraint, living within one’s means, and refusing free favours from strangers
Cold drinks were banned on buses
She hated town shopkeepers
The drink was stale
e: Even at age eight, Valli practiced impressive self-control and dignity by declining free treats from an acquaintance.

q: In the phrase "a source of unending joy" from "Madam Rides the Bus", what is the best antonym for "unending"?
o: Continuous
Temporary / brief
Boundless
Delightful
e: "Unending" means perpetual or ceaseless, so its opposite is "temporary" or "brief".

q: What does the adverb "commandingly" convey about Valli as she stopped the bus?
o: She was begging weakly
She looked shy and hesitant
Despite her tiny hand, she signalled with mature authority and complete confidence
She was waving goodbye
e: The contrast between her "tiny hand" and raising it "commandingly" charmingly highlights her confident personality.

q: What poetic effect do the words "clatter", "clank", and "jangling" produce when Custard attacks the pirate?
o: Lullaby-like calm
Gentle drizzle
Deadly silence
Vivid auditory imagery (onomatopoeia) conveying metallic power, ferocious motion, and dramatic action
e: The burst of onomatopoeic sound words brings Custard’s sudden, fierce metallic-sounding assault vividly to life.

q: Which combination correctly lists the temptations Valli sacrificed to save sixty paise?
o: Peppermints, toys, balloons, and riding the merry-go-round at the village fair
A bicycle and radio
Lunch and milk
New dresses and books
e: The text explicitly notes she resisted every temptation to buy peppermints, toys, balloons, and even ride the merry-go-round.

q: Valli originally calculated being home around 2:45 p.m., yet she reached her village at 3:40 p.m. Why does the narrative timing extend slightly?
o: Because the return bus left town after a stopover and took time back along the route, arriving at 3:40 still within her 1–4 p.m. window
Because the bus broke down for three hours
Because Valli caught the wrong bus to Delhi
Because her watch stopped
e: Even with town stopover and return boarding delays pushing arrival to 3:40 p.m., she still returned safely before 4 p.m.

q: In "and the blue, blue sky" from "Madam Rides the Bus", what effect does repeating the word "blue" create?
o: It represents midnight darkness
It captures the child’s breathless, pure wonder at the vast, vivid expanse of sky
It is a typographical error
It shows heavy air pollution
e: Repeating "blue" echoes the natural, breathless delight of a child marveling at wide-open horizons.

q: When Custard calmly agrees that everyone else is braver than him after eating the pirate, how does the reader interpret his statement?
o: Yes, he regretted eating the pirate
No, he didn’t understand English
Yes, he truly was the biggest coward
No—his quiet humility exposes the comical hypocrisy of the boasting pets even more sharply
e: After saving everyone, Custard’s refusal to argue for credit highlights his genuine humility against their hollow boasting.

q: Which poetic device is used in "Mustard was as brave as a tiger in a rage"?
o: Oxymoron
Pun
Apostrophe
Simile
e: Comparing Mustard’s supposed bravery using "as brave as a tiger in a rage" is a Simile.

q: Which action before the pirate’s arrival proves the other characters mistreated gentle Custard?
o: They threw him out of the house
Belinda tickled him unmercifully while Ink, Blink, and Mustard mocked him as Percival from the red wagon
They clipped his wings
They hid his food bowl
e: Their collective mocking and teasing from the red wagon show how boastful peers mistreat quiet, unassuming individuals.

q: Why did Valli dislike being called "child" by the elderly man and questioned by the elderly woman on the bus?
o: Because she wanted free food
Because she had planned, saved, and paid full fare like everyone else and took pride in managing herself independently
Because she forgot her birthday
Because she was actually twenty years old
e: Having planned every detail and paid full fare, she resented being patronised and insisted she could take care of herself.

q: In "The pirate gaped at Belinda’s dragon", what does the verb "gaped" mean?
o: Smiled warmly
Yawned sleepily
Leapt gracefully
Stared with mouth wide open in shock or amazement
e: "Gaped" means stared open-mouthed in shock—the pirate was stunned when the supposedly timid dragon charged fiercely.

q: In "The Tale of Custard the Dragon", what does Belinda’s quick embrace of Custard followed by returning to the old boasting status quo suggest?
o: Belinda forgot Custard’s name
The pirate haunted the white house
Custard flew away the next morning
People often offer fleeting gratitude in moments of relief, yet swiftly slip back into old vanities and biases once safety returns
e: It slyly highlights how people thank a saviour in the heat of relief, only to revert right back to familiar vanity and stereotypes.

q: What thematic connection can be drawn between Valli’s desire to ride the bus in "Madam Rides the Bus" and the broader idea of curiosity/freedom in First Flight?
o: The irrepressible urge to step beyond familiar thresholds (a front doorway) and experience the wider world directly
Hatred toward modern cities
Destroying village roads
Losing money on every trip
e: Stepping beyond her familiar threshold mirrors the universal urge to explore, assert independence, and claim firsthand experience.

q: Why is the elderly man’s warning ("you shouldn’t stand like that. Sit down.") sympathetic from an adult view yet understandably frustrating for Valli?
o: He hated the conductor
He genuinely worried a child might fall in a moving bus, whereas Valli felt patronised as someone who had paid full fare like everyone else
He wanted to steal her window seat
He feared the bus ceiling would collapse
e: Vallikkannan keeps both sides realistic: genuine parental concern from the elder clashed naturally with Valli’s fierce desire to be seen as grown-up.

q: Why does Ogden Nash keep repeating "little pet dragon" even while listing Custard’s fearsome teeth, spikes, and daggers?
o: Because he was made of plastic
Because he only woke at midnight
It sustains the humorous juxtaposition between a fierce mythical beast and an affectionate, domestic house pet
Because Custard was literally one inch tall
e: Calling a fire-breathing dragon a "little pet" keeps the tone whimsical and emphasises his gentle heart beneath spiky scales.

q: How did Custard’s actual crisis response refute his reputation as a coward in "The Tale of Custard the Dragon"?
o: He jumped out the back window
He bribed the pirate with grog
He stayed weeping in a corner
Instead of hiding, he alone sprang into decisive action against an armed intruder, proving true bravery shows when danger actually hits
e: True courage doesn’t advertise itself in calm times; it steps up instinctively when loved ones face real danger.

q: Why was Valli’s silence upon returning home at the end of "Madam Rides the Bus" wiser than bragging to her mother and aunt?
o: Revealing it would invite scolding/restrictions, and she instinctively knew her private bittersweet experience didn’t need validation from chatter
She temporarily lost her voice
The conductor threatened her
Her aunt spoke only French
e: Silence protected her freedom while preserving a deeply personal, bittersweet memory too precious for idle chatter.

q: How does the brand-new bus in "Madam Rides the Bus" function as a symbol for young Valli?
o: It represents an ancient fort
It acts as a gleaming bridge connecting Valli’s quiet rural street to modern mobility, novelty, and wider horizons
It symbolises agricultural ruin
It shows the conductor owned the village
e: Passing every hour, the gleaming bus served as Valli’s gateway from quiet routine into the thrilling wider world.

q: In "Belinda tickled him, she tickled him unmercifully", what attitude of Belinda toward Custard does "unmercifully" suggest?
o: She rushed him to a vet
She begged him for forgiveness
Though framed playfully, it shows she relentlessly teased his gentle nature without sparing his feelings
She plotted to poison him
e: "Unmercifully" highlights how relentlessly and carelessly everyone picked on Custard’s mild temperament.

q: Which civic value does Valli’s insistence—"I’ve paid my thirty paise like everyone else"—express at a young age?
o: Travelling without tickets
Reserving seats only for elders
Disobeying traffic rules
Equality and dignified self-assertion—fair rights apply equally regardless of age when one pays one’s fair share
e: She instinctively grasps fairness and equal dignity: paying full fare entitles her to equal respect regardless of age.

q: If "The Tale of Custard the Dragon" were staged as a drama, where does its decisive climax occur?
o: When Ink and Blink boast on the stairs
When everyone flees the armed pirate and Custard charges heroically to gobble him up
When Belinda buys a red wagon
When Mustard licks Custard’s nose
e: That decisive clash shatters every hollow boast and reveals Custard’s hidden heroism.

q: What inspiring quality does Valli share with other courageous young female protagonists in Class 10 NCERT English?
o: Disregard for learning
Sharp curiosity, independent thinking, sturdy self-respect, and the courage to step beyond narrow expectations
Passive obedience without thinking
Lifelong fear of stepping outside
e: Like other strong young NCERT heroines, Valli combines fearless curiosity with self-respect and independent grit.

q: How do both "Madam Rides the Bus" and "The Tale of Custard the Dragon" explore contrasts between expectations/appearances and reality?
o: Both end with pirates winning
Both insist young ones can never act wisely
Small Valli proves far wiser than patronising adults (while discovering death beneath joy), and "cowardly" Custard proves the sole true hero among boasters
Both chapters focus solely on village fairs
e: Both works overturn superficial judgements: tiny Valli exhibits rare maturity (and faces harsh reality), while timid-looking Custard outshines every boaster.
